ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Wichita, KS plants, tanks, piping and structural steel. Mobilized crews. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Wichita, Kansas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Wichita, Kansas for ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection on storage tanks, process and utility piping, pressure vessels, structural steel and plant equipment. We have no office in the city, so the crew travels to your site, works to your procedure or ours, and sends a report your inspector can act on. To scope a job, request a UT quote for Wichita and tell us the asset, the wall thickness and the code.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Wichita

Wichita is an aircraft-manufacturing city first. Textron Aviation, Spirit AeroSystems, Learjet and Airbus all have operations here, and the Greater Wichita Partnership counts more than 450 suppliers working around them. What that means for ultrasonic work is less obvious than the airframes themselves. Behind every production floor sits a utility plant: compressed-air receivers, steam and hot-water systems, chilled-water loops, fuel storage and the large pressure vessels used to cure composite parts. Those assets lose wall to corrosion like any other steel, and an ultrasonic thickness survey is how an owner learns how much is left.

The same survey logic applies to the older industrial stock that grew up with Wichita's oil history. Oil discoveries in nearby Butler County in the 1910s pulled refining and energy offices into the city, and the region still carries tank farms, gathering and transmission piping, and rail-served terminals. Add grain handling, food processing, hangar and plant structural steel, and the steel in the flood-control and river crossings that Wichita depends on, and the list of ultrasonic candidates is long and varied.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

Two jobs dominate. The first is thickness measurement: a transducer sends a sound pulse into the steel, the instrument times the echo from the back wall, and the reading tells you remaining wall at that point. The second is weld examination with an angle beam, which sends shear waves into the weld and heat-affected zone to look for lack of fusion, cracks, slag and incomplete penetration that a surface method cannot see.

Ultrasound does not see everything. Thickness readings describe the spot under the probe, so a pitted floor or a patch of under-deposit corrosion can hide between grid points. Rough scale, thick coatings, curved small-diameter pipe and coarse-grained cast or heavily worked material all weaken the signal. Laminations can send a straight beam to the wrong depth. A Level II technician plans around these limits and tells you where the data is thin; the report is only as honest as its stated coverage.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply in Wichita

The method follows the code that governs the asset. For ultrasonic examination of welds, ASME Section V Article 4 sets the examination method, while the construction code supplies the acceptance limits: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel groove welds, and API 1104 where pipeline welds are involved. Contact thickness gauging is covered by ASTM E797 and the thickness provisions of Article 23 in Section V. Our guide to ultrasonic thickness requirements explains the calibration and documentation points in plain terms.

Kansas has its own boiler safety act in Chapter 44, Article 9 of the Kansas statutes, and that act lists exemptions, among them certain refinery equipment inspected in-plant and pressure vessels built before 1999. Whether a given vessel falls under the act is a question for the owner and the jurisdiction. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and reports the data, such as thickness at condition monitoring locations, for that inspector to evaluate.

How the work is done

For thickness surveys, the technician calibrates on a step block made of the same material, using a dual-element probe where the outside surface is corroded and a single-element probe on clean, smooth wall. The A-scan display stays on screen so the technician can reject doubled echoes and see when a reading is really a lamination. On hot lines, a high-temperature probe and couplant are used and the readings are corrected for temperature. Readings are taken at marked condition monitoring locations so the next survey can repeat them exactly.

Weld work starts with a procedure written to the code, a calibration block, and a reference level built from side-drilled holes. The technician scans from both sides where access allows with 45, 60 or 70 degree angle beams, marks every reflector that crosses the reporting threshold, then characterizes length and position before comparing to the acceptance table. Surface preparation, grinding of weld crowns and clean scanning lanes decide whether that scan can be trusted.

Thickness surveys in practice: grids, corrosion rates and remaining life

A one-time reading tells you where the wall is today. A repeated reading at the same marked spots tells you how fast it is going, and that rate is what turns a number into a decision. On a storage tank, utility vessel or piping circuit, the usual plan is a grid on the shell or floor course, readings at every condition monitoring location on a line, and extra points around nozzles, elbows, tees and low points where water and deposits collect. Corrosion rate is the change in thickness divided by the time between readings, and remaining life is the margin above minimum required thickness divided by that rate. The calculation belongs to the owner's engineer or authorized inspector; our job is to deliver readings that are repeatable enough to support it.

Repeatability depends on discipline. We mark each location with paint or a stamped tag, record the probe and couplant, and note whether the reading was taken through paint or on bare metal, because a coating can add apparent thickness if the instrument is not set up for it. When a reading looks low or erratic, the technician scans around the point to separate a true pit from a lamination or a poor couplant film, then records the minimum found in the area rather than only the single nominal location.

Weld examination: what the angle beam is really doing

Shear-wave examination is a matter of geometry. The probe wedge refracts the beam into the steel at a fixed angle, and the technician moves the probe in a controlled raster pattern while watching the display for echoes that line up with the weld. A reflector from lack of fusion at the bevel face shows differently from slag in the root or a crack at the toe, and an experienced Level II uses the beam path, the probe position and the echo shape together to decide what the signal really is. Geometry reflectors such as root reinforcement and weld crown can look like flaws, so the technician plots the signal position against a sketch of the joint before calling anything an indication.

Sensitivity is set from a reference reflector in a calibration block of the same material and thickness range. Scanning gain is then raised above reference to find small signals, and every indication above the reporting level is evaluated by amplitude and length. On heavier sections, more than one beam angle and scanning from both sides improve the chance of catching a flaw that is oriented unfavorably for one direction. Where the weld cap is left unground or the heat-affected zone is not accessible, the report states the loss of coverage.

Typical Wichita assets and the question each one raises

  • Compressed-air receivers and utility vessels: internal corrosion from condensate is the concern, so thickness at the bottom head and drain area matters most.
  • Composite cure autoclaves and process vessels: thickness checks of shell and heads at the intervals set by the owner's inspection program.
  • Above-ground storage tanks and fuel tanks: shell courses, bottom plate and roof, with the owner's authorized inspector deciding on fitness.
  • Plant and hangar structural steel: weld examination on repairs and modifications, and thickness where corrosion has attacked base metal.
  • Process and utility piping: thickness at elbows, tees, reducers and dead legs, plus weld examination on new and repaired joints.
  • Crane runway and support structures: weld checks after modification or when a fatigue concern has been raised.

Who does the work

Our technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the setup, calibration, examination and interpretation, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports before they leave. Report review sits with our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, which covers how we control documents and records, not the examination itself. If your site requires a customer-specific aerospace procedure, send it with the request and we will read it against our written practice before agreeing scope.

What the UT report contains

Every report identifies the component, the line or tag number, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, and the technician and level. For thickness work you get a grid or table of readings by location, nominal thickness, previous readings where they exist, and the minimum found. For weld work you get indication locations on a sketch, length, amplitude against the reference level, and an accept or reject call against the named criterion. Limitations such as inaccessible areas or a poor surface are written down rather than left for the reader to guess.

Planning a UT job in Wichita

Wichita weather shapes the schedule more than people expect. Summer brings days at or above 90 degrees about 65 times a year, with a few at 100, so hot steel and heat-affected technicians matter for exterior tank work. Winter lows are cold enough that couplant thickens and flaw detector screens slow down, and spring thunderstorms with hail and high wind can close a job at short notice. Aerospace plants and food plants add their own access rules: badging, foreign-object control, lockout and permits are normal. We ask for the safety orientation requirements, escort rules and permit process in the first call so crews arrive prepared. Travel is booked around your outage window, and the crew works from your site.

UT versus MT and PT for your Wichita job

Use ultrasound when the question is wall loss or what is inside a weld. Use magnetic particle testing in Wichita when the question is surface cracking on carbon or low-alloy steel, and liquid penetrant testing in Wichita when the material is non-ferrous or stainless and the concern is a surface-breaking flaw. Many inspection plans combine them: UT for the volumetric weld check, then MT or PT on the cap and toe. Our national pages on ultrasonic testing describe the method in general terms.

Training your own UT technicians

Plants with steady thickness work often prefer to qualify their own staff. We offer UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with a browser ultrasonic testing simulator for practice before hands-on time at your own facility, and a Wichita training page that explains how the delivery works. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel; we supply the training and the Level III oversight.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Wichita?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Wichita. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, work under the company's written practice, and report back with a document your own inspector can review and file.

faq.q: Can you measure wall thickness on tanks and piping in Wichita?
faq.a: Yes. We run ultrasonic thickness surveys on tanks, piping, vessels and structural steel, calibrated on a matching step block, with readings recorded at marked condition monitoring locations so later surveys can be compared point for point.

faq.q: Do you perform ultrasonic weld inspection?
faq.a: Yes. Angle-beam shear wave examination of groove welds is done to a written procedure, with a reference level built from side-drilled holes, and indications are compared with the acceptance table of the governing code before the report is issued.

faq.q: Which codes do your UT reports follow?
faq.a: That depends on the asset. Typical references are ASME Section V Articles 4, 5 and 23, ASME Section VIII Division 1, ASME B31.3 and B31.1, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, API 1104 for pipeline welds and ASTM E797 for thickness.

faq.q: Who is the inspector of record on API 510, 570 or 653 work?
faq.a: Your authorized inspector. Atlantis does not act as that inspector; we perform the ultrasonic examination, report thickness and indication data, and your inspector evaluates it against the applicable inspection code.

faq.q: What can stop ultrasonic testing from giving a good result?
faq.a: Heavy scale, thick coatings, rough weld caps, very small diameters, hot surfaces without suitable couplant and coarse-grained material all degrade the signal. We note these conditions and recommend surface preparation or a different method when they matter.

faq.q: How do I request a quote for ultrasonic inspection in Wichita?
faq.a: Use the quote link on this page or the contact form, and send the asset type, material, wall thickness, governing code, access constraints and your outage window. Expect our reply within one business day.

faq.q: Will you work to our own procedure or customer specification?
faq.a: Yes, if it fits the examination. Send the procedure or specification early; our Level III reads it against our written practice and tells you whether we can work to it, or what needs to be added, before any technician is mobilized.

faq.q: Can you train our technicians in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. We provide UT Level 1 and Level 2 training with Level III oversight and a simulator for practice. Qualification and certification stay with your company under its written practice, as SNT-TC-1A requires.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Wichita, KS | MT Testing
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) for welds, castings, structural steel and rotating equipment in Wichita, KS. Mobilized Level II crews. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Wichita, Kansas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Wichita, Kansas for magnetic particle inspection of welds, castings, forgings and structural steel on your site. Mag particle testing finds cracks and other discontinuities at or just under the surface of carbon and low-alloy steel, quickly and with simple equipment. We have no office in Wichita; crews travel to the plant, tank or fabrication floor. For a scoped proposal, request an MT quote for Wichita with the part, the code and the access conditions.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Wichita

The steel that holds Wichita's factories up is a natural MPI customer. Aircraft makers and their suppliers rely on heavy tooling, jigs, fixtures and overhead cranes, and that equipment lives at a stress level that eventually opens fatigue cracks at lugs, pin bores and weld toes. Hangars, hoists and lift trucks at the airports and plants carry the same risk. Structural steel in warehouse, plant and bridge work needs weld checks at fabrication and again after repair.

The energy side of the region adds more: pressure vessel nozzle welds, tank shell-to-bottom welds, pump and compressor supports, and the lifting lugs and trunnions on equipment that gets moved. Grain elevators, food and meat processing plants, and rail-served terminals use conveyors, drives and shafts where a surface crack grows quickly if no one looks. Magnetic particle work is the sensible first look at any of these ferromagnetic parts.

What MT finds and what it misses

The method magnetizes the part so that any crack crossing the field creates a small leakage that attracts fine iron particles. The indication shows up as a sharp line, usually within a minute of application. It works on ferromagnetic material only, which means carbon steel and most low-alloy steel, and it does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or titanium. It finds surface-breaking flaws and some shallow subsurface ones, but not deep embedded flaws.

Direction matters. A crack parallel to the magnetic field produces almost no indication, so each area is examined with the field applied in two directions at roughly right angles. Paint, thick scale, weld spatter and oil reduce sensitivity and can hide a small crack. Residual magnetism after the test can interfere with welding or damage bearings, so demagnetization is part of the procedure when it matters. The technician records both what was tested and what could not be reached.

Codes and acceptance criteria in Kansas work

Magnetic particle work is governed by ASME Section V Article 7, which covers the method, the equipment and the technique. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 gives methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 covers process piping, AWS D1.1 sets criteria for structural welds, and AWS D1.5 applies to steel bridges. For general industry, ASTM E1444 is the practice and ASTM E709 the guide. Our walkthrough of Article 7 requirements helps owners write a procedure that an examiner can follow.

The Kansas boiler safety act lists exemptions for some pressure equipment, including vessels built before 1999 and certain refinery equipment inspected in-plant. Confirm with the jurisdiction which category your vessel sits in. For API 510, 570 or 653 work the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection; Atlantis performs the examination and reports the crack indications found.

How the work is done

Field work usually uses an AC electromagnetic yoke, since it is portable and sensitive to surface cracks. A yoke must lift a defined test weight at the pole spacing in use, and the technician checks that lift before the job and keeps the record. For prods or a DC yoke, the same attention applies to current and pole spacing. Visible dry or wet particles work in normal light on a clean surface; fluorescent particles are used in a darkened area under UV-A light when higher sensitivity is needed on a critical weld.

The sequence is clean, magnetize, apply particles during magnetization, examine, record, and demagnetize if required. A field indicator or a pie gage confirms that the field is strong enough in the area under examination. The technician examines each area in two directions, marks relevant indications with a paint pen or photograph, and then evaluates them against the stated acceptance criteria.

Choosing a magnetizing technique for the part

The right technique depends on the shape and what you are looking for. A yoke is ideal for welds, plate edges and open surfaces because the field runs between the poles and can be turned ninety degrees for the second pass. Prods push current directly through the part and give a circular field around the current path, which suits thick weldments and castings, but they can burn the surface if the contact is poor, so many specifications restrict their use. Coils wrap a field around shafts and long parts, and central conductors suit bores and rings. For a crane hook or a pin, a combination of circular and longitudinal fields is often needed to reveal cracks in every direction.

Field strength is checked, not assumed. A pie gage or a shim indicator placed on the surface shows whether the field is strong enough to form an indication of the right sensitivity, and the technician moves the yoke so that overlap is adequate on every pass. On a long weld, the examiner works in overlapping segments, marks the boundaries, and examines each segment twice before moving on. This is slow-looking work, and it is what makes the result reliable.

Wet and dry particles: choosing between them

Dry powder is convenient on rough, hot or outdoor surfaces, and it is the common choice for field weld checks on structural steel. It is blown onto the part in a light cloud while the yoke is energized and is sensitive to larger surface cracks. Wet suspension particles, carried in water or oil, give much higher sensitivity to fine cracks and are the standard for critical welds and machined surfaces. The suspension is applied by spray while the field is active, and the bath concentration is checked with a settling test so the particle load is within the procedure's range.

Contrast matters as well. Black particles on a white contrast paint show up crisply on a clean weld, red or gray dry powders suit dark surfaces, and fluorescent particles in a darkened area under UV-A light reveal very fine indications that visible particles would miss. We choose the combination to suit your code, the surface and the access conditions, then write it into the procedure so the examination can be repeated later by someone else.

Typical Wichita parts and the cracking each one tends to develop

  • Overhead crane hooks, lugs and pad eyes: fatigue cracks in the throat, shank and eye after repeated lifts.
  • Tooling and fixture welds: toe cracks and cracks at repair welds where heat input was high.
  • Pressure vessel nozzle and attachment welds: cracks from thermal cycling and from weld shrinkage stress.
  • Tank shell-to-bottom and nozzle welds: cracks at stress concentrations, especially where settlement has occurred.
  • Shafts, couplings and drive components: fatigue cracks at keyways, fillets and shoulders.
  • Structural connections: weld cracks at beam-to-column joints and brackets after overload or impact.

Each of these calls for different access and a different field direction, which is why a scope that names the parts is more useful than one that only says magnetic particle testing.

Reading indications correctly

Not every particle line is a crack. Magnetic writing from contact with another magnet, changes in section, sharp fillets, the edge of a weld and the boundary between weld metal and base metal all collect particles in lines that look serious and are not. A trained Level II separates relevant indications, which come from real discontinuities, from nonrelevant ones, which come from the shape or magnetic properties of the part. When in doubt, the technician cleans the area, demagnetizes, and repeats the test with a different technique or direction. Indications that stay are measured and compared with the acceptance table: linear indications are usually evaluated by length, and rounded ones by size and spacing.

Who does the work

Our crews are qualified under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the equipment, performs the test and evaluates indications; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the final report. Procedures here are approved by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. We follow your customer's procedure when it is provided, and our written practice development service is available if your own program needs updating.

What the MT report contains

The report states the part or weld identification, the material and surface condition, the procedure and revision, the magnetizing method, the particle type and carrier, the yoke or equipment identification with its last verification, the technician and level, and the date. Indications are listed with location, orientation and size, sketched or photographed, and each is dispositioned as accepted or rejected against the code. Areas not examined are called out, so the reader is never left wondering whether a corner was reached.

Planning an MT job in Wichita

Wichita's hot, humid summers make heat a factor for fluorescent work in enclosed areas, since darkening a space often means shutting out ventilation. Cold winter days can make surfaces damp or frosted, which affects particle suspension; a clean, dry surface is the first requirement. Spring storms with hail and wind can close exterior work, and tornado warnings stop all field activity on most sites. Plants may require orientation, badging, hot-work or confined-space permits before a crew can begin. We ask for site rules in the first call and plan the mobilization around your outage and access windows.

MT versus UT and PT for your Wichita job

Magnetic particle testing is usually the fastest way to check carbon and low-alloy steel for surface cracking. If the metal is stainless, aluminum or another non-magnetic material, liquid penetrant testing in Wichita is the usual choice. If you need to know about wall loss or about flaws inside a weld, ultrasonic testing in Wichita answers a different question. Our MT versus PT comparison and the national page on magnetic particle testing go deeper on how to choose.

Training your own MT technicians

If your plant does regular crack checks on crane hooks, tooling and weld repairs, it may make sense to train your own examiners. We provide MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, the Wichita training page explains how delivery and practical work are arranged, and our NDT practice tests help candidates prepare. The employer certifies its own technicians under SNT-TC-1A.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials, mainly carbon steel and low-alloy steel. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or titanium; for those materials liquid penetrant testing is normally used to find surface-breaking cracks.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Wichita?
faq.a: No. We have no office in Wichita. Level II technicians travel to your plant, tank, fabrication floor or yard with the equipment needed for the agreed scope, and report back under our written practice.

faq.q: Can MT find cracks under paint?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded coatings may be tolerated if the procedure allows it, but thick paint, scale or weld spatter reduce sensitivity. The procedure states the limit, and the technician may ask for coating removal before examination.

faq.q: Why is each area examined in two directions?
faq.a: Flux that runs along the length of a crack barely disturbs it, so the flaw hides. Examining with the field at roughly right angles in a second pass makes sure cracks in any orientation have a chance to show up.

faq.q: Do you use fluorescent or visible particles?
faq.a: Both are available. Visible particles are common for routine weld checks in normal light, while fluorescent particles under UV-A light in a darkened area give higher sensitivity for critical welds, as the procedure and code require.

faq.q: Is demagnetization necessary after testing?
faq.a: Sometimes. Residual magnetism can interfere with later welding, machining or bearing operation, so the procedure calls for demagnetization when those risks apply, and the report records whether it was done and how it was checked.

faq.q: Which standards do your MT reports follow?
faq.a: Typical references are ASME Section V Article 7, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, ASME B31.3, AWS D1.1 and D1.5, and ASTM E1444. The report names the procedure and the acceptance criteria that were applied.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for MT in Wichita?
faq.a: Send the part or weld description, material, surface condition, governing code and access details through the contact form or the quote link on this page. We reply within one business day with questions or a proposed scope.

faq.q: Can you train our staff in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes. We offer MT Level 1 and Level 2 training with Level III oversight. Your company writes its own written practice and certifies its own technicians; we help with the program, the training and the examinations.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Wichita, KS
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for welds, castings and non-ferrous parts in Wichita, KS. Mobilized Level II crews. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Wichita, Kansas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Wichita, Kansas for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, of welds, machined parts, castings and fabricated assemblies. Penetrant testing finds cracks, laps and porosity that are open to the surface, on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-porous materials where magnetic methods do not work. We have no office in the city; crews travel to your site. To scope a job, request a PT quote for Wichita and describe the material, surface and code.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Wichita

Wichita's industrial base is built on aircraft, and aircraft-related manufacturing uses a great deal of metal that is not magnetic: aluminum structure, titanium fittings, stainless tubing and nickel-alloy hardware. Textron Aviation, Spirit AeroSystems, Learjet and Airbus anchor the region, and the supplier network behind them machines, welds and repairs those materials every day. A site that handles such parts often needs surface-crack checks that do not depend on magnetism.

Outside aerospace, penetrant work appears in food and beverage plants where stainless vessels and piping carry strict hygiene demands, in chemical and energy equipment made of stainless or duplex alloys, and in weld repairs on pressure parts. Welded fixtures, tooling, pump housings and machined castings all come through shops in the region. When the question is simply whether a weld toe or a machined edge has an opening to the surface, PT is a direct answer.

What PT finds and what it misses

The method depends on capillary action. A low-viscosity penetrant is applied to a clean surface, held for a dwell time so it can enter any opening, removed from the surface, and then drawn back out by a developer that makes the flaw visible. Only discontinuities that are open to the surface can be found. A crack closed by peening, smearing, machining or heavy blasting may not draw penetrant, and a subsurface flaw never will.

Surface condition is everything. Oil, paint, scale, weld flux and previous penetrant residue block entry and cause false or missing indications. Porous materials absorb penetrant and produce a background that hides defects. The technician states the cleaning method, because a good result starts with a surface that has been properly prepared and dried. Where the part cannot be cleaned adequately, PT is the wrong method and the report says so.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply in Kansas

ASME Section V Article 6 defines how penetrant examination is performed, while the construction code supplies acceptance. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 sets methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 covers process piping, and ASTM E165 is the common practice for general industry. Weld repairs in structural work may reference AWS D1.1. See our explanation of Article 6 requirements for the procedure details owners need to specify.

The Kansas boiler safety act exempts certain refinery equipment inspected in-plant and some older vessels, so confirm the status of your equipment with the jurisdiction. Where API 510, 570 or 653 governs, the owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record. Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and reports the surface indications found, which the inspector then evaluates.

How the work is done

Penetrant materials are chosen to suit the part. Type II visible, color-contrast penetrants are used in normal light, and Type I fluorescent penetrants are used under UV-A light in a darkened area when higher sensitivity is required. Solvent-removable systems dominate field work because they travel well; water-washable and post-emulsifiable systems appear on shop-style jobs. Sulfur and halogen content is controlled for work on nickel alloys and stainless steel, and technicians check the lot certifications.

The steps are pre-clean, apply penetrant, hold the dwell, remove excess without washing out the flaws, apply a thin even developer, wait for the development time, and examine. The technician keeps surface and penetrant temperature inside the procedure's range, evaluates indications as they bleed out, and records them. A final cleaning removes developer after inspection when later coating, welding or service demands it.

Penetrant families, sensitivity and removal methods

Penetrant systems are classified by how they are seen and how they are removed. Type I fluorescent penetrants glow under UV-A light and give the highest sensitivity; Type II visible penetrants show as a red indication against a white developer in ordinary light. Removal comes in four methods, lettered A through D, running from plain water wash through the two emulsifier systems to a solvent wipe. Field work is mostly Method C because the cleaner, penetrant and developer come in cans that travel well and need no water supply or drain. Shop work on larger quantities of small parts often uses water washable or post-emulsifiable systems because the throughput is better.

Sensitivity levels run from low to ultra-high and apply to fluorescent systems. A higher level reveals tighter cracks, but it also picks up more background on a rough surface, so a critical machined part and a rough weld cap are not examined with the same system. We select the system to match your procedure and the surface, and we record the product family, manufacturer and lot in the report so the examination can be repeated.

Dwell time, removal and developer: where the technique succeeds or fails

Dwell time is how long the penetrant stays on the surface before removal. Too short and the penetrant does not reach tight cracks; too long and it dries and cannot be removed cleanly. The procedure sets a minimum and, for most systems, a maximum. Removal is where more flaws are lost than anywhere else: over-wiping with solvent washes penetrant out of a shallow crack, and under-wiping leaves a background that hides small indications. The technician wipes with a lint-free cloth lightly dampened with solvent, working in one direction and checking the surface under suitable light before moving on.

Developer is applied in a thin, even coat. Too thick a coat can mask fine indications, while too thin a coat does not draw enough penetrant to the surface. Developer time is held for the period in the procedure, and the examination begins while indications are still forming so that the technician can watch bleed-out and judge whether a feature is a crack, a pore or a surface irregularity. Then a final examination is made once the development time is complete.

Typical Wichita parts and what penetrant testing is asked to find

  • Aluminum and titanium components: cracks at fastener holes, fillets, machined edges and weld repairs, under the customer's own requirements.
  • Stainless steel vessels and piping in food and process plants: weld cracks and pinholes in sanitary and chemical service.
  • Nickel-alloy hardware and exhaust-type fabrications: cracks from thermal cycling at welds and flanges.
  • Machined castings and housings: shrinkage cracks, cold laps and porosity opened by machining.
  • Weld repairs on carbon steel: final check of a ground-out and re-welded area before it returns to service.
  • Tooling and fixtures: surface cracks at welds on non-magnetic or coated assemblies.

When a part is both magnetic and critical, many owners use both methods, with MT first for speed and PT as a confirming check on a repair.

Reading and recording indications

Penetrant indications are described by their shape. A linear indication, longer than three times its width, usually points to a crack, lap or seam. A rounded indication is typically porosity or a pit. A continuous line of small dots can mean a tight crack that is bleeding in places. The technician measures the length of each relevant indication, notes its position from a reference point on the part, photographs it when the procedure calls for it, and then compares it with the acceptance table in the governing code. False indications from lint, spilled penetrant, rough surfaces or contamination are identified and cleared, and doubtful areas are retested after recleaning so that the final report stands on a clean examination.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the part or weld, material, surface condition and prior processing, the procedure and revision, the penetrant family and manufacturer with lot numbers, the cleaning and removal method, dwell and development times, the surface temperature, and the technician and level. Each indication is located, measured, photographed or sketched, and dispositioned as accepted or rejected against the named criteria. Areas that could not be cleaned or examined properly are recorded as such.

Planning a PT job in Wichita

Temperature is the main planning constraint. The standard range in ASME Section V Article 6 is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials, and a procedure qualified for another range is needed outside it. Wichita sees many afternoons above 90 degrees from late spring through early fall, so sun-heated steel can run well beyond the limit, and winter mornings can sit below it. We plan exterior work for shade, early hours or enclosures, and check surface temperature with a contact thermometer. Plant access, hot-work permits and storm cancellations are part of any Wichita schedule, and we build the mobilization around your window.

PT versus MT and UT for your Wichita job

Choose penetrant testing for non-magnetic metals and for any surface-breaking flaw question where magnetic particle is not an option. For carbon steel with a clean surface, magnetic particle inspection in Wichita is often faster. For internal weld quality and wall loss, ultrasonic testing in Wichita is the right tool. The national page on penetrant testing and our MT versus PT comparison cover the trade-offs in more detail.

faq.q: What does liquid penetrant testing detect?
faq.a: Only discontinuities that are open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, seams and porosity. Subsurface flaws and cracks that have been closed by smearing or peening will not draw penetrant and will not be found.

faq.q: Which materials can be tested with dye penetrant?
faq.a: Any non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys and carbon steel. It is the usual choice where magnetic particle testing cannot be used because the metal is not ferromagnetic.

faq.q: How hot or cold can penetrant testing be done?
faq.a: The standard window in ASME Section V Article 6 is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. Outside it, the procedure has to be qualified for the temperature, so we measure the surface before starting.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much?
faq.a: Oil, paint, scale and flux fill or cover openings and stop penetrant from entering. A poorly cleaned surface gives missed indications and false ones, so cleaning method and dryness are recorded in every report.

faq.q: Should I use visible or fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible color-contrast penetrant is practical in normal light for routine field work. Fluorescent penetrant viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area is more sensitive and is chosen when the code or the part criticality calls for it.

faq.q: Are penetrant materials controlled for stainless steel and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes. Sulfur and halogen content is limited for those materials, and our technicians check the lot certification of the penetrant, cleaner and developer before use and record the lot numbers in the report.
